title: Optional visits with penalties, and pickup and delivery

blocks.text: 4.8.4 Optional Visits With Penalties, and Pickup and Delivery

Two of the Valley's four inspection crews are called away to storm repairs, and the two that remain cannot inspect all 18 substations in one shift. The eight urgent sites (five years or less of predicted life) must still be done today; the ten routine ones can wait for next week, but the planner would rather skip the ones whose failure would cost least. Lesson 4.8.2 showed what a plain routing model does when the work does not fit: it finds nothing, and says only that it timed out. This lesson makes the routine visits optional, at a price, so a plan always exists and the price decides what gets skipped.

The same afternoon, a second request arrives: the portable transformer test set was left at substation A157, and the crew inspecting A230 needs it. Some crew must collect it at A157 and carry it to A230. That is a **pickup and delivery** pair, the second half of this lesson. The drive times are fictional, as everywhere in this module.
A Disjunction With a Penalty Makes a Visit Optional

The routing library's tool for "this visit may be skipped" is the **disjunction**: a set of indices of which at most a given number (by default one) are visited. With a penalty, each index of the set that is left out adds the penalty to the objective. A disjunction holding a single index is exactly "visit this site, or pay to skip it". The OR-Tools dropped-visits guide makes all 16 of its locations optional this way:

# Allow to drop nodes: one disjunction per location, each holding that one location.
penalty = 1000
for node in range(1, len(distance_matrix)):
    routing.AddDisjunction([manager.NodeToIndex(node)], penalty)
Three rules come from `AddDisjunction`'s docstring:

items: **The list holds indices, not nodes**, so convert with `NodeToIndex`.
**The depot, and every vehicle's start and end, cannot be in a disjunction.** The loop starts at node 1 for that reason.
**A site with no disjunction is mandatory.** That is how the Valley model keeps the urgent sites: it gives a disjunction to the routine sites only.

blocks.text: The docstring adds a fourth rule: **a negative penalty makes the disjunction mandatory**. The penalty must be positive for the visit to be optional; a negative one forces the visit, so `AddDisjunction([index], -1)` keeps the site just as leaving it out of every disjunction does. That is handy when the penalties come from data and a must-visit site is marked with a negative number. `negative_penalty.py` runs the two-crew Valley day of the next section twice, with A183's penalty at 10,000 and at -1:

for label, a183 in (("A183 penalty 10000", 10_000), ("A183 penalty -1", -1)):
    penalty = lambda site: a183 if site.name == "A183" else 10_000
With a penalty of 10,000, A183 is among the seven dropped sites; with -1 it is on crew 1's route, and seven other routine sites are dropped instead.
The guide's data has demands that add up to 70 for four vehicles of capacity 15 (60 in all), so at least 10 units of demand must be dropped:

Objective: 7548
Dropped nodes: 15 16 (demand 16)
vehicle 0: 0 -> 8 -> 14 -> 9 -> 0  load 15
vehicle 1: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 11 -> 12 -> 0  load 13
vehicle 2: 0 -> 7 -> 13 -> 0  load 14
vehicle 3: 0 -> 5 -> 6 -> 2 -> 10 -> 0  load 12
distance 5548 + 2 x 1000 = 7548

The objective is the distance plus 1,000 per dropped node. The guide's page shows a different answer, nodes 6 and 15 dropped for 7,936. Its program stops the search after one second; this copy stops it after 100 solutions. Both are plans the model accepts, from searches that ran for different lengths, and how a search is stopped is lesson 4.8.5's subject.
The Penalty Decides What Gets Dropped

The penalty is the price of skipping a visit, in the objective's units (here meters or drive minutes). The solver drops a site whenever dropping it saves more than its penalty, and that one fact sets the rule for choosing penalties. The dropped-visits guide states it: a penalty larger than the sum of all arc costs means dropping a visit can never pay for itself, so the solver drops only what it must to make the plan feasible. A smaller penalty lets it drop a visit just because it is out of the way.
`valley_drops.py` runs the Valley day four ways, with vans of 12 kits:

policies = [
    ("two crews, penalty 10000 each", 2, lambda site: 10_000),
    ("two crews, penalty cof // 10", 2, lambda site: site.cof // 10),
    ("three crews, penalty 10000 each", 3, lambda site: 10_000),
    ("three crews, penalty cof // 100", 3, lambda site: site.cof // 100),
]

all arcs of the drive matrix add up to 8334 minutes
low-priority sites (cof $k): A064 523, A091 2577, A096 2505, A133 291, A149 661, A183 2978, A281 2241, A302 210, A305 3516, A344 1843
two crews, penalty 10000 each: objective 70176 = drive 176 + penalties 70000
  dropped 7: A091, A133, A149, A183, A281, A302, A344
  crew 0: A348 > A064 > A106 > A308 > A087  back 14:17
  crew 1: A157 > A378 > A136 > A096 > A230 > A305  back 15:50
two crews, penalty cof // 10: objective 1062 = drive 229 + penalties 833
  dropped 7: A064, A091, A133, A149, A281, A302, A344
  crew 0: A305 > A087 > A230 > A136 > A378  back 15:51
  crew 1: A157 > A348 > A106 > A308 > A096 > A183  back 15:04
three crews, penalty 10000 each: objective 283 = drive 283 + penalties 0
  dropped 0: none
  crew 0: A096 > A106 > A302 > A281 > A305 > A344 > A133 > A183  back 14:53
  crew 1: A378 > A157 > A149 > A348 > A136  back 13:22
  crew 2: A087 > A064 > A091 > A308 > A230  back 15:12
three crews, penalty cof // 100: objective 244 = drive 215 + penalties 29
  dropped 3: A064, A281, A302
  crew 0: A087 > A305 > A344 > A133 > A183  back 12:25
  crew 1: A378 > A157 > A149 > A348 > A136  back 13:22
  crew 2: A096 > A106 > A091 > A308 > A230  back 15:12
Read the runs as business policies:

items: **Penalty 10,000 for every routine site** is above the 8,334-minute sum of all arcs, so no drop pays for itself in driving. With two crews, all eight urgent sites are kept (they have no disjunction), and seven routine ones are dropped. With equal penalties, the solver has no reason to prefer one routine site over another, so which seven go is decided by geography: it kept A064, A096 and A305.

**Penalty proportional to the consequence of failure (cof)** says what the planner means: skipping a transformer whose failure costs $3.5M is worse than skipping one that costs $0.2M. Seven sites are still dropped, but now A183 (cof 2,978) is kept and A064 (cof 523) is dropped.

**A penalty that is too small** (cof // 100, 2 to 35 minutes) breaks the plan in the other direction. With three crews and a penalty of 10,000, the solver visits all 18 sites in 283 drive minutes, so three crews can do the whole day. With cof // 100 it drops A064, A281 and A302 anyway, for penalties of 5, 22 and 2 minutes (29 in all), because the plan without them drives 215 minutes: 68 minutes saved for 29 paid. Those three transformers go uninspected to save fuel.

blocks.text: A penalty is a trade-off rate between two things the objective adds up. Put both in the same units, check that the largest saving a drop could bring cannot exceed the penalty of a site you must not lose, and when nothing may be skipped, leave the site out of every disjunction.
A Dropped Visit Is an Index That Points to Itself

A dropped site is on no route, and the routing model encodes that by making it its own successor: $`\text{next}_i = i`$. So you find dropped visits by testing every index that is neither a start nor an end, as the guide's printer does:

The start test matters: a start index is never a visit, even when its vehicle is unused (then it points to its end). The ends lie past `routing.Size()` (lesson 4.8.1's index table), so the loop never reaches them; the `IsEnd` test only makes the intent plain.

The penalty a plan paid is the sum of its dropped sites' penalties, and the objective minus that sum is the driving. `valley_drops.py` prints the split on every line ("drive 229 + penalties 833"), and a planner should get the same split: a total of 1,062 means little until you know how much of it is fuel and how much is risk left in the field.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Pickup and Delivery Is a Pair, a Same-Vehicle Row and an Order Row

The test set must be collected at A157 and taken to A230. The pickup and the delivery are two visits with two rules between them: **the same crew** does both, and it reaches **the pickup first**. The OR-Tools pickup-and-delivery guide writes each rule as one constraint, plus a call that tells the search the two visits belong together:

for pickup_node, delivery_node in pickups_deliveries:
    pickup_index = manager.NodeToIndex(pickup_node)
    delivery_index = manager.NodeToIndex(delivery_node)
    routing.AddPickupAndDelivery(pickup_index, delivery_index)
    # The same vehicle does both stops ...
    routing.solver().Add(routing.VehicleVar(pickup_index) == routing.VehicleVar(delivery_index))
    # ... and reaches the pickup first (the distance driven so far is smaller there).
    routing.solver().Add(distance_dimension.CumulVar(pickup_index) <= distance_dimension.CumulVar(delivery_index))

items: `routing.solver()` is the constraint-programming solver under the routing model, and `Add` posts a constraint on its variables directly. This is how you write a rule that no dimension or disjunction expresses.
`routing.VehicleVar(i)` is the vehicle that visits index $`i`$; equal vehicle variables put both stops on one route.
The order row compares cumuls of a dimension that only grows along a route (distance driven), so "smaller cumul" means "earlier on the route". A time dimension works the same way.
`AddPickupAndDelivery(pickup, delivery)` declares the pair. Its docstring says it helps the search, especially local search, which then moves both stops together.

blocks.text: The guide's eight items and four vehicles, from this module's adapted copy:

Each pair from the data sits on one route in order: [1, 6] on vehicle 3, [2, 10] and [5, 9] on vehicle 1, [4, 3] on vehicle 2. The search here starts from `PARALLEL_CHEAPEST_INSERTION`, the guide's choice for this problem (lesson 4.8.5 compares strategies).

Which of the three calls does what? `valley_test_set.py` builds the Valley pair three ways and asks the model to accept or refuse three hand-built plans. `routing.ReadAssignmentFromRoutes(routes, True)` takes one list of nodes per vehicle (depot left out) and returns `None` when the plan breaks a rule, which makes it a direct test of a model:

AddPickupAndDelivery with both rows:
  one crew, pickup then delivery         accepted
  one crew, delivery then pickup         refused
  pickup by crew 0, delivery by crew 1   refused
AddPickupAndDelivery with same-vehicle row left out:
  one crew, pickup then delivery         accepted
  one crew, delivery then pickup         refused
  pickup by crew 0, delivery by crew 1   accepted
AddPickupAndDelivery with order row left out:
  one crew, pickup then delivery         accepted
  one crew, delivery then pickup         refused
  pickup by crew 0, delivery by crew 1   refused

The result in OR-Tools 9.15: `AddPickupAndDelivery` by itself already refused the delivery before the pickup, but it **accepted a plan in which crew 0 collects the test set and crew 1 delivers it**, which no crew could carry out. Only the same-vehicle row refuses that. So write both rows, as the guide does: the order row states the rule in your model rather than leaving it to a declaration, and the same-vehicle row is the one the plan cannot do without.
The solved Valley plan:

objective 851
  crew 0: YARD > A348 > A136 > A106 > A308 > A087 > YARD
  crew 1: YARD > A157 > A378 > A230 > YARD
Crew 1 collects the test set at A157 and delivers it at A230, two stops later. (The objective includes a span coefficient of 10 on the Drive dimension, so it is not the drive time alone.)
<!-- practice 2 -->
The Model

The Valley model with optional visits that `valley_model.build` makes when it gets a `penalty`, and the pickup-and-delivery rows of `valley_test_set.py`. Lessons 4.8.1 to 4.8.3 gave routes, Kits and Time; this lesson added the disjunctions and the pair. It is a vehicle routing model, searched by the routing library's heuristics.

**Sets.** $`N`$ the nodes, node 0 the yard and 1 to 18 the sites; $`U \subseteq N`$ the urgent sites; $`R = N \setminus (U \cup \{0\})`$ the routine sites; $`V`$ the crews; $`I`$ the indices; $`P`$ the pickup-delivery pairs $`(p, d)`$ (one pair, A157 to A230, in `valley_test_set.py`).
**Parameters.** As in lesson 4.8.3 ($`c_{ab}`$, $`\text{service}_a`$, $`[a_i, b_i]`$, $`H`$, $`W`$, $`k_a`$, $`K`$), plus $`\pi_i > 0`$, the penalty for skipping routine site $`i`$.
**Variables.** As in lesson 4.8.3, plus $`\text{active}_i \in \{0, 1\}`$ for each site index: 1 if a route visits it. A site with $`\text{active}_i = 0`$ has $`\text{next}_i = i`$.
**Objective.**

\min \; \sum_{i \in I \setminus \{e_v\},\ \text{active}_i = 1} c_{\text{node}(i),\, \text{node}(\text{next}_i)}
\; + \; \sum_{i \in R} \pi_i \,(1 - \text{active}_i)
**Constraints.**
Summary

items: **A disjunction with a penalty makes a visit optional.** `AddDisjunction([index], penalty)` per optional site; a site with no disjunction, or with a negative penalty, stays mandatory; the depot can never be in one.

**The penalty decides what gets dropped.** The solver drops a site when the saving exceeds the penalty. Above the sum of all arc costs, it drops only what it must; proportional to value, it drops the least valuable; too small, it drops sites it could have visited.
**A dropped visit is an index that points to itself.** Test `solution.Value(routing.NextVar(i)) == i` for every index that is neither a start nor an end, and report penalties apart from driving.
**Pickup and delivery is a pair, a same-vehicle row and an order row.** In OR-Tools 9.15, `AddPickupAndDelivery` alone accepted a pair split across two vehicles; the same-vehicle row refuses it.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: visit `i` or pay `penalty`; a negative penalty makes it mandatory
visit at most `max_cardinality` of the set; pay per missing one
declares a pickup-delivery pair for the search
posts any constraint on the routing variables
a hand-built plan as an assignment, or `None` if the model refuses it

Challenges

items: In `valley_drops.py`, give the urgent sites a disjunction too, with a penalty of 100,000. Predict what changes with two crews.
Two substations sit on the same feeder, and inspecting either one is enough. Write it as one disjunction of two indices.
The test set must be delivered before 11:00. Which dimension and which call express that?

blocks.text: Design Note: Penalties Turn "Infeasible" Into "Here Is What It Costs"

A model with hard visits answers a short fleet with nothing (lesson 4.8.2). A model with penalties always has a plan (drop everything is one), and it answers a different, better question: "with the crews I have, what is the least painful set of visits to postpone?" The price of that answer is that the penalties are now part of the model, and a planner must agree to them. Write them in business terms (here, a share of the consequence of failure), show the dropped list next to the routes, and treat "seven sites postponed" as a result to explain, not a detail.
